title: 6 Best Devin Alternatives in 2026
summary: Devin alternatives compared by where the agent runs and what a unit of work costs: Awesomic, Factory, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Claude Code and OpenHands.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- In Pinna et al.'s MSR 2026 study of 7,156 reviewed agent PRs, Devin's PRs merged 61.6% of the time against 77.9% for OpenAI Codex, but the PRs date back to late 2024 and Devin alone was improving week over week, so treat that gap as dated.
- 4 of the 6 Devin alternatives can run the delegated agent on infrastructure you control, with conditions: OpenHands self-hosts free, Copilot needs a self-hosted Actions runner, Claude Code's route is a Team and Enterprise beta, and Factory runs on your machine through Remote Control. Awesomic and Codex cloud use only the vendor's computers, while Devin's Outposts already run on your hardware.
- Each competitor's cheapest plan with its cloud agent is listed at $20 a month or less: Copilot Pro is the lowest paid one at $10, and OpenHands is $0 to self-host with your own model key.
- Devin Pro is $20 a month on a quota Cognition doesn't publish in numbers, pooled across Devin Cloud, Devin Desktop and the CLI.


Devin is Cognition's autonomous software engineer. You hand it a ticket from Slack, Jira or Linear, it works in its own cloud VM, and it comes back with a pull request. Teams start looking at Devin alternatives when the quota runs dry midweek, when they want a different model mix, or when a ChatGPT or Claude plan they already pay for could cover the same work.


One naming note first. On June 2, 2026, Cognition renamed its Windsurf editor to Devin Desktop, so one price card now covers both. This article covers Devin the cloud agent, not the editor.


Each entry is judged on three questions: how you hand off a task, where the agent runs, and what you pay per unit of work. A fourth matters to some teams: whether a person can finish what the agent starts, which is the idea behind[pairing agents with humans](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/agents-humans-awesomic-supernova) . Every price was rechecked on the vendor's own site on November 13, 2026.


## Why teams look for Devin alternatives


Cognition pitches Devin as "your team's autonomous software engineer," which it says works in the cloud or on your machine, does its testing in its own browser and keeps going until the PR is ready to merge.


Devin spins up its own Linux and Mac VMs, plus Windows ones on a limited basis, runs parallel cloud agents, takes work from Slack, Teams, Jira, Linear and PagerDuty, and opens PRs on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket. For a team that files a ticket and wants a branch back, that's a complete loop.


The friction sits in the meter. Pro costs $20 a month and Max $200, with daily and weekly quotas on Pro and a weekly one on Max, but Cognition doesn't publish the quota numbers. The quota is shared across Devin sessions, the CLI and Devin Desktop, so a heavy editor day eats into cloud runs. Past it, you buy prepaid on-demand credits that roll over.


That model is new. On April 14, 2026, Cognition announced it was retiring the Core and Team plans, whose old Team entry point was $500 a month, and moving self-serve overage from Agent Compute Units to dollars.


Users feel the ceiling. In[one Reddit thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/DevinAI/comments/1xi44pk/is_devin_worth_it/) , a user calls Devin's cloud "by far the best cloud offering" but says most plans "don't give you enough tokens to do much," while another keeps 10 or more sessions going, sometimes overnight, and checks them from a phone, so heavy use is possible. Both are user reports. The first points back to the meter: with no published quota, you can't predict when you'll need credits.


Review is the other friction point. A finished-diff workflow puts all the checking at the end, which is where agent PRs stall.[Ehsani and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15195) studied 33,000 agent PRs on GitHub and found each additional failed CI check cut the odds of a merge by about 15%.


Of 600 sampled unmerged PRs, 38% were abandoned by reviewers, the most common pattern, ahead of duplicates at 23% and CI or test failures at 17%. So review is a data-backed reason to switch if the new tool changes how you review, while cost rests on user reports. The intro's other reasons are matters of fit rather than data.


## What the merge-rate data says about handing off tasks


The closest thing to a head-to-head comes from[Pinna, Gong, Williams and Sarro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08915) at the MSR 2026 Mining Challenge, covering 7,156 closed, reviewed agent PRs in permissively licensed repos. Both studies here use the same AIDev dataset of public agent PRs.


Devin's 2,252 PRs in that sample merged 61.6% of the time. OpenAI Codex reached 77.9%, Cursor 74.5%, Claude Code 71.9% and GitHub Copilot 68.0%, though Claude Code's figure rests on just 139 PRs and the authors say to read it with caution. Devin was the only agent trending upward, gaining about 0.77 points a week over 32 weeks.


Task type mattered about as much as which agent wrote the PR. Documentation PRs averaged an 82.1% merge rate and new features 66.1%, a 16-point spread close to the gap between Codex and Devin, so compare tools on the same tickets.


Keep the dates in mind. The PRs run from late 2024 onward, so treat Devin's gap as a dated reading to test, not a reason to switch on its own. Codex led the sample, but its cloud tasks run only on OpenAI's own VMs, reason enough for some teams to weigh[Codex alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/codex-alternatives) too.


## The best Devin alternatives compared


Awesomic is first because it's our product. After that, the order runs from the closest Devin-shaped product (assign a ticket from your tracker, get work done on a managed cloud machine) to the most hands-on (an open-source agent you host yourself). Instead of a rating, the last column shows where the agent runs.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


The pricing column shows each agent's cheapest route as covered here; team prices are in the cost section.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Running parallel agents, with an optional expert hand-off


**Overview:**[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) lets several AI agents work on one project at once, each in its own chat on shared files, with vetted human experts in the same app.


As with Devin, agents run in parallel on a cloud machine that works with your laptop shut, but here each project gets its own, with up to 1 TB of storage, and you can follow it from the browser, desktop apps or iOS and Android apps. Every chat can run Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode, picked per task.


The difference shows up when output needs a professional: you hand the task to a vetted expert in the same chat, who sees the files and everything the agents did.


**Key features:**


- Parallel agents on shared files, so a fix and its tests move at once.
- One bill across four agents, so you switch when one stalls.
- 1,000+ app connections, including GitHub and Slack, plus a shared team keychain.
- Admin-set budgets and approved models, plus a view of spend per person.


**Pricing:** Studio is $499 per person per month, and as on every tier, that price is also the month's AI budget. Light at $19, Basic at $99 and Pro at $199 carry the same agents and models.


People cost extra. All-in-One runs $3,219 a month and covers no-code development, design, copywriting and quality checks, while a Dedicated expert, for example a vetted developer, is priced on a call. Both include a Light seat.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** four agents from different vendors on one bill, expert hand-off with full context, an optional bring-your-own Claude or Codex plan


**Cons:** not a dedicated ticket-to-PR engineering agent (Jira and Linear connect only as apps), no published coding benchmark, budget-based usage pricing without a published per-model rate, expert help billed as a separate plan


**How to start using it:**


1. Buy an agentic plan for each person who'll run agents.
2. Create a project and its cloud computer.
3. Connect GitHub and add shared keys.
4. Open one chat per task and choose its agent.
5. Add an expert plan when a person needs to finish the work.


**Why it's a good Devin alternative:** Devin hands back a pull request, while here a vetted expert can finish what the agents start. We accept 0.82% of the experts who apply and can match you with one in as little as 24 hours, which fits when the deliverable is a launched site or app, not a merged branch.


**Final verdict:** Choose Awesomic for parallel agents on a per-project machine with an expert plan as backup; for Jira-driven ticket-to-PR automation, the next entry fits better.


### 2. Factory


**Overview:** Factory's agents, called Droids, take work the way Devin does: you assign an issue in Linear or Jira, or mention @Factory in Slack or Teams. Droids run in reusable cloud Environments, on persistent Droid Computers that auto-pause when idle, on your own machine through Remote Control, or in the local CLI.


**Key features:**


- OpenCompute provisions sandboxes in your own cloud account, though it's a private preview you have to request.
- Missions turn multi-feature work into a plan you follow in Mission Control.
- Automations start on a schedule, a Slack message, a GitHub event or a webhook, so recurring fixes need no ticket.


**Pricing:** A Free plan runs on your own model key; assigning tickets needs Pro. Pro is $20 a month, Plus $100 with about 5x Pro usage, Max $200 with about 10x, and Teams $60 a month per team plus $40 a seat, up to 10 seats. Usage is counted in Factory Standard Credits under rolling 5-hour, 7-day and 30-day limits, and Extra Usage is prepaid credit with a $10 minimum and no expiry.


**Pros:** delegation from Slack, Linear, Jira or Teams, a choice of Factory's cloud or your own machine, a free open-weight Droid Core pool after you hit a limit


**Cons:** Missions require Extra Usage and pause at a rate limit, Teams caps at 10 seats


**Why it's a good Devin alternative:** Factory keeps Devin's ticket-in, work-out hand-off, with Missions for work that spans several features.


**Final verdict:** Pick Factory if you like Devin's workflow and want a fallback model pool that keeps Droids working, outside Missions, after you hit a limit.


### 3. GitHub Copilot


**Overview:** Copilot in the cloud is GitHub's hand-off agent, and its new version reached paid plans on October 28, 2026. You assign work from Slack, Teams, Jira, Linear or Azure Boards, then choose where it runs: a GitHub-hosted Linux sandbox by default, an Actions job on a hosted or self-hosted runner, or your own Linux machine or codespace, a route that still needs the prerelease CLI and custom-environment access.


**Key features:**


- Sessions resume across web, mobile, VS Code and the CLI.
- A self-hosted Actions runner keeps the job on hardware you manage.


**Pricing:** For $10 a month, Pro carries 1,500 AI credits, Pro+ is $39 with 7,000, Max $100 with 20,000, Business $19 a seat with 1,900 and Enterprise $39 a seat with 3,900, with overage at $0.01 a credit. Part of those credits is a flex allotment GitHub says may change. Cloud sandboxes first use your GitHub plan's included compute allowance, worth $12 a month on GitHub Free and $18 on GitHub Pro, then bill at $0.000024 per compute-second, $0.000003 per GiB-second of memory and $0.005 per GiB-month of snapshot storage.


**Pros:** the lowest paid entry price on this list, a self-hosted runner option, Azure Boards as a hand-off source


**Cons:** two meters to watch (compute comes with a monthly allowance), not available on Free, Actions sessions take a single repo and start only on the GitHub website


**What it does best:** It keeps working after the PR opens: Agent Merge watches the PR and fixes failing Actions checks and merge conflicts, the failed-CI problem the Ehsani study tied to lower merge odds.


**Final verdict:** Go with Copilot if your code already lives on GitHub and you want either tracker hand-offs or runs on your own runners.


### 4. OpenAI Codex


**Overview:** Codex cloud keeps everything on OpenAI's side: each task runs in its own OpenAI-hosted VM and keeps going while your laptop sleeps. You start work from the web, CLI, IDE, iOS app, Slack or a Linear issue assigned to Codex, and an AGENTS.md file in the repo tells it which lint and test commands to run.


**Key features:**


- Bigger plans get bigger VMs: 2 vCPU, 8 GiB of RAM and 8 GiB of disk on Plus, and 4 vCPU, 16 GiB and 32 GiB on Pro, Business and Enterprise, with larger ones available to Enterprise.
- Saved VM state is recoverable for up to 7 days, and OpenAI's older cloud docs say agent internet access is off by default.
- Mentioning @Codex on GitHub triggers an automatic PR review, and the CLI is open source under Apache-2.0.


**Pricing:** Plus, at $20 a month, is the first plan listing cloud tasks, Pro runs $100, $200 or $500 a month, and Business is $20 per user per month billed annually or $25 monthly, with a two-user minimum. Allowances come in ranges, such as 15 to 160 GPT-6.1 Sol local messages per 5 hours on Plus, and cloud tasks can draw more from them before ChatGPT credits take over.


**Pros:** works inside a ChatGPT plan many teams already pay for, PR review from a GitHub mention


**Cons:** Free and Go don't list cloud tasks and an API key gets no cloud features, usage given as ranges with no fixed task count, Plus VMs stop at 8 GiB of RAM


**Where it fits:** Codex posted the highest merge rate in the Pinna sample at 77.9% across 12 weeks of PRs from mid-2025, and it still led when only the weeks all five agents share are compared, which earns it a trial on your own tickets.


**Final verdict:** Choose Codex when you'd rather extend a ChatGPT plan than add a vendor, and can live with an allowance stated as a range.


### 5. Claude Code


**Overview:** Claude Code's cloud sessions run in a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VM per session on Anthropic's infrastructure, with 4 vCPU, 16 GB of RAM and 30 GB of disk. Team and Enterprise organizations can also run them in a self-hosted environment, a public beta that's off by default. You start one from the browser, your phone, the desktop app or` claude --cloud` , and` --teleport` pulls it back to your terminal.


**Key features:**


- PR auto-fix through the Claude GitHub App, so follow-up fixes land on the same PR.
- Parallel sessions plus scheduled or triggered runs.
- A network allowlist by default, so the VM can't reach arbitrary hosts.


**Pricing:** Pro is $20 a month or $17 billed annually, Max $100 for 5x Pro usage, and Ultra $200 with 10x Pro's weekly usage and no 5-hour limit for verified accounts. Team is $20 a seat per month billed annually, and Enterprise adds usage charges and a 20-seat minimum. Below Ultra, limits run in 5-hour and weekly windows, unpublished as numbers and shared with chat and local Claude Code.


**Pros:** pull a cloud run into your terminal mid-task, a self-hosted beta on Team and Enterprise


**Cons:** Anthropic-hosted cloning and PR creation need GitHub, with GitLab and Bitbucket going as a local bundle or through the self-hosted beta, Claude models only, no cloud sessions for Zero Data Retention, HIPAA or CMEK organizations


**Why teams shortlist it:** It changes how you review rather than how much: instead of checking a finished diff, you watch a run and interrupt it when it drifts, which still takes a reviewer's time.


**Final verdict:** Choose Claude Code if you want to watch and steer cloud runs and you're fine on Claude models only.


### 6. OpenHands


**Overview:** OpenHands is the open-source end of the list. Agent Canvas is free and MIT-licensed to self-host, and you bring your own LLM key. It runs on your laptop by default, or in Docker, a VM, Modal, DigitalOcean sandboxes or OpenHands Cloud sandboxes.


**Key features:**


- Run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or OpenCode inside it, so one setup covers several agents.
- Automations from GitHub, Slack, Jira, Linear or a schedule handle PR review, CI-failure fixes and triage.
- GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Slack integrations, with new releases every few days.


**Pricing:** Self-hosting costs $0 plus your model bill, and Teams is $500 a month for up to 10 users plus $50 a month per extra seat, with SSO/SAML, budgeting, a 30-day trial and a cap of 5,000 sessions a month. Enterprise is custom, and OpenHands Cloud has no plan price; its docs list per-million-token model prices passed through with no markup, some of them free.


**Pros:** free MIT license, any model through your own key, runs anywhere from a laptop to your own cloud


**Cons:** you run and secure the infrastructure, the $500 team floor sits above Devin Teams' $80, no plan price for OpenHands Cloud


**Why it made this list:** OpenHands is the only entry you can run end to end without paying the vendor anything, which suits teams that must keep the agent itself in-house.


**Final verdict:** Pick OpenHands if someone on staff can run the infrastructure and you want full control over models and hosting.


## Pros and cons of switching from Devin


For some teams, the biggest gain is a meter you can read. Copilot is the clearest, publishing per-credit and per-second rates, while a self-hosted OpenHands install has no vendor meter at all.


Hosting is a smaller gain than it looks, because Devin's Outposts already run sessions on your own VMs, containers, Kubernetes or a Mac Mini, with the agent loop in Cognition's cloud. Devin Enterprise adds VPC deployment on top.


Another gain is how you review. In a[Reddit comparison of Pro plans](https://www.reddit.com/r/windsurf/comments/1v0vrnw/my_experience_comparing_the_pro_plans_devin_vs/) , the poster reported that Claude's 5-hour window gave about as much work as Devin Pro's weekly limit, and a commenter noted that Devin hands you a finished diff while Claude Code lets you watch and interrupt. Treat both as user reports.


What you may lose is breadth. Devin takes PagerDuty triggers, boots Mac and, on a limited basis, Windows VMs, and opens PRs on GitLab or Bitbucket, while Claude Code's Anthropic-hosted sessions need GitHub and Copilot's Actions sessions take a single repo.


Switching also reopens a bigger question: whether an agent should own the work at all. If nobody has time to review agent PRs, compare[freelancers, agencies and subscriptions](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/freelancers-vs-agencies-vs-subscriptions-startup-guide) before you buy more seats.


## How much Devin alternatives cost


Headline prices hide the unit each vendor actually meters, so the table below sets Devin beside all six alternatives on price and on that unit.


GitHub is the only vendor in that table that publishes a per-second compute rate, which makes it the easiest to model. By our estimate, an hour of sandbox time runs about $0.09 in compute plus $0.09 per 8 GiB of memory once the plan's compute allowance is used, before AI credits. GitHub's sandbox overview prices compute per vCPU-second, so bigger sandboxes may cost more.


Most of the rest ask you to trust a window or a budget. If you'd rather pay a fixed monthly cost for finished work than watch a usage meter, a flat[development subscription](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/unlimited-development-subscription-why-is-it-worth-it-for-scaleups-and-enterprises) is a different way to buy the same outcome.


## How hard is it to move off Devin?


Most of a move is wiring: re-creating Devin's triggers and Git connections, then proving the new tool on real tickets. Plan on two weeks of overlap:


1. List every place Devin takes work from today, such as Slack channels, Jira projects, Linear teams or PagerDuty.
2. Check that the new tool supports your Git host, because Claude Code's Anthropic-hosted sessions need GitHub for cloning and PRs.
3. Write your setup, lint and test commands into a file the agent reads, such as AGENTS.md for Codex.
4. Re-create the triggers, for example a Linear assignment for Factory or an Azure Boards hand-off for Copilot.
5. Run both agents on the same 10 tickets for two weeks and compare merged PRs and review time.
6. Use up any prepaid on-demand credits left on Devin before you cancel.


The overlap gives you merge numbers from your own repos, not a public dataset. If it shows your team would rather keep the agent in its own terminal, one of the local[Aider alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/aider-alternatives) skips the trigger wiring altogether.


## Mistakes to avoid when comparing Devin competitors


The first mistake is comparing sticker prices. Copilot's $10 plan looks cheapest but has two meters, and Claude Code's $20 plan shares its windows with chat, so price each tool on a week of your real tickets.


The second is skipping where code runs. Organizations on Zero Data Retention, HIPAA or CMEK can't use Claude Code's cloud sessions, and Codex cloud tasks run only on OpenAI's VMs. If compliance decides hosting, start from the comparison table's last column.


The third is treating open source as free. OpenHands costs $0 to self-host, but you pay for the model key, the servers and the person who secures them. Among Devin competitors, it has the cheapest license and the most to run yourself.


The last is forgetting review capacity. Abandoned PRs were the top failure pattern in the Ehsani sample, so 20 agent PRs a week only help if someone reviews 20 PRs a week. If nobody has time to run the comparison, outside[AI consulting services](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/ai-consulting-services) can scope it for you.


## How to choose the right Devin alternative


Start from the problem that sent you looking, since each reason to leave Devin points to a different entry:


- If the unpublished quota is the problem, GitHub Copilot publishes per-credit and per-second rates.
- If code must stay on infrastructure you control, check Devin's Outposts first; if the agent itself must stay in-house, OpenHands self-hosts fully and Copilot can use your own Actions runner.
- If you already pay for ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro or a higher tier, Codex or Claude Code adds cloud tasks to that plan.
- If you want another model mix, OpenHands takes any model through your own key.
- If you'd rather review as the agent works than face a finished diff, Claude Code lets you follow a run and cut in.
- If failing CI checks stall your PRs, Copilot's Agent Merge fixes them.
- If you like Devin's ticket hand-off as it is, Factory takes assignments from Linear, Jira, Slack or Teams.


Team size narrows it further. Factory's Teams plan stops at 10 seats and OpenHands Teams covers 10 users before extra seats, while Claude Code Enterprise needs at least 20 seats and Devin Teams runs up to 100 users.


Awesomic admins can set per-person budgets and an approved-model list before any agent touches your code, and enterprise teams can add[on-demand support](https://www.awesomic.com/enterprise) on top.


## Which agent to hand your next ticket to


Pick one Devin alternative from the list and run the two-week overlap test against Devin. Try a second only after the first test ends, on the same tickets, so you never review three agents' PRs at once. Merged PRs, review time and cost from your own tickets settle more than any comparison table can.


Weight the result by your task mix, and check each agent's hosting against your compliance rules before you sign. If you want several agents on one project, you can[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) with one plan per person and bring in an expert plan once a job needs a person.


## FAQ


### What is the closest alternative to Devin?


Factory is the closest match. Its Droids pick up issues from Linear or Jira, or a Slack or Teams mention of @Factory, and work on a Factory-managed cloud machine or your own, with own-cloud sandboxes in private preview. Pro starts at $20 a month, the same as Devin Pro.


### Is there a free Devin alternative?


OpenHands is free and MIT-licensed to self-host, so you pay only for the model key and the machine it runs on. Factory also has a Free plan on your own model key, though ticket hand-offs start on Pro. Codex has Free and Go plans, but Plus is the first one that lists cloud tasks, and Copilot in the cloud isn't on GitHub's Free plan.


### Does Devin still bill in ACUs?


Only on Enterprise. Since the change Cognition announced on April 14, 2026, self-serve overage is billed in dollars, so Pro, Max and Teams run on a quota plus prepaid on-demand credits. Enterprise ACUs are billed at your order-form rate.


### What are the main Devin competitors in 2026?


Besides our own entry, the five tools covered here are Factory, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Claude Code and OpenHands. Factory is closest in workflow, Copilot and Codex sit inside plans many teams already pay for, Claude Code lets you steer runs, and OpenHands is the self-hosted option.


### Is Devin Desktop the same thing as Devin?


No. Devin Desktop is the editor formerly called Windsurf, renamed on June 2, 2026, while Devin is the cloud agent you delegate tickets to. They share one Cognition price card and one pooled self-serve quota.
